The northern army surrounds every valley. Inside, the ministers argue all day: fight, or kneel. On the fifteenth night a young officer, {npc}, climbs alone to the highest wall and asks the mountain whether help is coming. It is not.

choices.text: "No help is coming. Tell the king the truth"

mem.note: told me the truth on the wall

effects.log: {npc} goes down and tells the king, and is beaten for it by a minister who wanted to hear something else. But the king remembers, later, who told the truth.

choices.text: Warm the fortress: hold the worst of the cold off the walls

effects.log: The snow falls on the besiegers and melts on the walls. Nobody inside freezes that winter. They will still run out of rice. But they do not freeze.

choices.text: Break the siege yourself

ok.log: You come down on the northern camp like an avalanche. Their horses run to the river. The army withdraws a week's march to reconsider. It is a reprieve, not a victory, and the king knows it, and so do you.

fail.deathCause: the northern army's cannon, in the snow below the fortress
fail.log: They have brought cannon.

events.text: The forty-fifth day. The grain is gone. The king comes out of the fortress gate in a plain blue robe, as a subject, and walks down to the riverbank, where the northern emperor sits on a nine-step platform. There the king will kneel three times and bow nine times. {npc} walks behind, shaking, and looks up at you.

choices.text: Let it happen. The kingdom will live, humbled

effects.log: Three kneelings. Nine bows. The sound of the royal forehead on the frozen ground carries a long way in the quiet. The kingdom lives. The king never smiles again. {npc} remembers every sound for years.

choices.text: Darken the sky over the ceremony, so all know heaven is grieving

effects.log: The ceremony takes place under a black noon sky. The northern emperor hurries it. Afterwards, in every village, they say even heaven would not watch. It is a small thing. It is not nothing.

choices.text: Promise {npc}: "I will remember the cold, and the kneeling, and who did it"

effects.log: {npc} nods, unable to speak. Two years later the conquerors make the kingdom raise a stone on the riverbank praising their emperor's virtue. You remember the truth underneath it.

events.text: Long years later, the stone on the riverbank praising the conquering emperor has been pulled down, buried, dug up, and stood up again in a park, where children climb on the stone turtle that carries it. The northern empire is gone. So is the kingdom that knelt. The fortress walls on your ridge are a place where old people walk in the autumn.

choices.text: Tell the walls' story to a child who asks

effects.log: The cold, the forty-five days, the young officer on the wall. The child listens, then runs to the end of the wall to look at the view. That is what the walls are for now. It is a good use.

choices.text: Let the walls be a walk in the autumn and nothing more

effects.log: Grief has a shelf life even for something as old as you. You find, on the ridge in the autumn, that you have finally put it down.

events.text: A great army has crossed the sea from the east and taken the southern ports in a fortnight. The capital has fallen. The king has fled north. In the temple below your mountain an old abbot, {npc}, has put down the rosary and picked up a staff, and is calling the monks of eight provinces to fight. "I know it is against the precepts," {npc} says to your summit. "Tell me if it is against you."

choices.text: "It is not against me. Go. I will watch your roads"

effects.log: Five thousand monks march out of the mountains. For seven years no ambush ever catches them on a mountain road. They fight, they nurse, they bury, and the righteous armies follow them.

choices.text: "Pick up the staff. But carry the wounded first"

effects.log: {npc} makes it the order of the monk army: the wounded of both sides, first. It is the only army in the war that does it. Their enemies learn to surrender to monks.

choices.text: "The precepts are older than this war. Keep them"

effects.log: {npc} bows and stays in the temple, and the temple becomes a hospital, and then it is burned. {npc} lives. Many of the monks who stayed do not.

events.text: The enemy fleet is coming up the narrow strait, three hundred ships against thirteen. The admiral of the thirteen has chosen the strait for its current, which turns hard at the change of the tide. If it turns early, the thirteen are lost. If it turns at the right moment, the three hundred are.

choices.text: Hold the tide until the moment is right

ok.log: You hold the whole sea still for one long hour, and then let it go. The current turns into the enemy's faces. Thirteen ships hold the strait. The admiral never knows, and writes in a diary that night only that the sea was kind.

fail.log: You cannot hold it. The current turns when it turns. The admiral had counted on it anyway, to the minute. The thirteen win without you, and you learn something about human courage. (-15 health)

choices.text: Leave the sea alone. The admiral counted on the real tide

effects.log: The admiral was right. The current turns exactly when the old fishermen said it would. The thirteen hold the strait. It is entirely a human victory, and better for it.

choices.text: Rise from the strait in front of the enemy fleet

effects.log: The lead ships see something in the water and turn, and the ships behind them collide. It is a disaster in a narrow place. The admiral of the thirteen sees it too, and says nothing about it in any report.

events.text: Seven years of war are over. The enemy has gone home across the sea. Half the farmland is waste, the palaces are ash, and in the temple below your mountain {npc}, very old now, is carving names onto a memorial stone: monks, farmers, soldiers, and at the bottom, in smaller characters, the enemy dead buried on the mountain too.

choices.text: Help carve the names, through the night, in the stone

effects.npcPass: old age, in the temple, after the war
effects.log: The names are cut deep and clean, more than any one carver could manage in a night. {npc} finds them in the morning and sits down in front of the stone. That is where {npc} dies, the next spring, very peacefully.

choices.text: Bring rain for the waste fields, to start the first harvest

effects.npcPass: old age, in the temple, after the war
effects.log: The first harvest after the war is thin, but it comes. {npc} lives to see it, and dies before the second, satisfied.

events.text: The kingdom you have watched for ages is ending. Its last king, old and tired, has decided to give the realm to the rising kingdom in the north rather than see the capital burned. The king climbs to the royal tombs on your slope to tell the ancestors, and, since you are there too, tells you.

choices.text: "You save a million lives with one shame. It is a good trade"

effects.log: The king weeps on the tomb steps. Then the procession goes north, three hundred carts and the crown on a cushion. The capital does not burn. It becomes a provincial town, and lives.

choices.text: "So long a kingdom should not end with a surrender. Fight"

effects.log: The king looks up at you for a long time, then shakes the old head. "I am too old to make a widow of every house for my pride," the king says. The procession goes north anyway. You are, for once, ashamed.

choices.text: Say nothing, and bow to the last king of a long line

effects.log: The king sees the vast shadow bow on the mountain, and bows back. Nobody else ever knows. In the north, the new court treats the old king with honour. It is the best end a kingdom can have.

events.text: The crown prince would not surrender. {npc} has left the capital in clothes of rough hemp, and is walking to the diamond mountains in the far north-east to live in a hut on the rocks, eating grass, until death. {npc} stops at your mountain on the way, because {npc} played on its slopes as a child.

choices.text: Walk {npc} to the diamond mountains

mem.note: walked with me to the diamond mountains

effects.log: You go as a shadow on the road, and nobody bothers a prince in hemp clothes. At the mountains, {npc} sits on a rock and says, "This is far enough." The hemp-clad prince lives there forty years. The pilgrims still find the hut.

choices.text: "Stay. Your people need someone to remember them who is not their conqueror"

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it all night on your slope and goes north anyway at dawn. "You will remember them," {npc} says. "You remember everything." It is not exactly a compliment.

events.text: The old capital is a quiet town of rice fields and grave mounds as big as hills. Farmers plough around the royal tombs, and one of them has found a gold crown in a furrow, hung with jade and leaves of beaten gold that tremble at a touch. Nobody alive remembers the kingdom it belonged to except you.

choices.text: Tell the farmer whose it was

effects.log: The farmer, who is a practical person, listens, then reburies it, very carefully, in the same tomb. "The king might want it," the farmer says. The crown waits another thousand years.

choices.text: Let the farmer take it to the magistrate

effects.log: The crown goes to the new court and then to a treasury, and then, much later, behind glass, where people stand for a long time looking at the trembling gold leaves. You find you like that.

events.text: A temple stood in the valley below you for five hundred years. A war burned it; a dynasty that disliked monks did not rebuild it. Now there is a market day in its old courtyard every five days, around the one stone pagoda that survived. A fishmonger leans against the pagoda to sell dried pollack. Nobody remembers the temple's name.
events.arc: The Temple That Became a Market

choices.text: Make the pagoda chime on market days, once, at noon

effects.log: A single clear note, from nowhere, every fifth day at noon. The market adopts it as its clock within a year. It becomes the noon bell of the valley, without anyone ever asking what rings it.

choices.text: Let the market be a market

effects.log: The monks chanted here for five hundred years. Now the fishmongers shout. Both are prayers of a sort. You listen to both.

choices.text: Whisper the temple's name to the fishmonger

effects.log: The fishmonger is startled, and then tells everyone, and the market takes the old temple's name. It is the only thing that survives of it, apart from the pagoda.

events.text: The market around the pagoda has become a town. The town has become a county seat. There is a magistrate's office where the monks' kitchen was, and a school where the sutra hall stood. A boy at the school is writing an essay on the pagoda for the examination, and has come to the foot of your mountain to think.
events.arc: The Temple That Became a Market

choices.text: Give the boy the temple's whole history in a dream

effects.log: The essay is so detailed that the examiners accuse the boy of copying a lost book. There is no lost book. The boy passes anyway, on the strength of the poetry.

choices.text: Let the boy find it alone

effects.log: The boy gets most of it wrong and writes it beautifully. It becomes the official history of the town. You are the only one who knows it is wrong, and you decide that is fine.

events.text: The county seat is a ruin now in its turn: a later war, a moved road, a river that changed its bed. Weeds in the magistrate's yard. And in the middle of it all, the stone pagoda, unbroken, three towns old, with an old woman leaning on it selling dried pollack, as if nothing had happened.
events.arc: The Temple That Became a Market

choices.text: Buy a fish. Somehow

effects.log: You leave a silver coin from a dynasty five hundred years dead on her mat at night. She takes it to a scholar in the next town and is suddenly comfortable for the rest of her life. That is, you decide, the price of a fish.

choices.text: Watch the stone pagoda outlast another age

effects.log: You and the pagoda are the only two things here that remember all three towns. It does not speak. You do not need it to.

events.text: Mago Halmi, the giant grandmother who made the mountains by carrying rocks in her skirt, is walking across the peninsula again, which she does every few thousand years to tidy up. Her skirt has a hole in it. Rocks are falling out of it into the paddies of a village below, each one the size of a house.

choices.text: Catch the rocks before they land

ok.log: You catch eleven of them and set them down gently on the hill. The grandmother notices and pats you, which knocks the wind out of you for a week. The eleven rocks are still on the hill. They have names now.

fail.log: You catch four and the fifth catches you. The village is spared; you are not, quite. The grandmother apologises in a voice like an avalanche. (-12 health)

choices.text: Tell her about the hole

effects.log: She looks down, startled, and laughs, and sits down on a mountain to mend it with a pine. While she sews, she tells you how she made the sea. It takes a hundred years. It is the best story you have ever heard.

choices.text: Let the rocks fall. She made this land; she can remake it

effects.log: The rocks fall in the paddies. The village moves up the valley. In a thousand years the rocks are called the Grandmother's Droppings and children climb them on festival days. The land does not mind being remade.

events.text: The grandmother has come back to sit on your mountain. She is tired, and her skirt is empty, and she is thinking of lying down for good and becoming a range. "Peer," she says, "when I am a mountain, who will tell the villages I was a grandmother?"

choices.text: "I will"

effects.log: She lies down along the southern horizon and becomes a range with a soft profile like a sleeping face. You tell every village, for a thousand years, who that is. They still call it the Grandmother.

choices.text: "Do not lie down yet. There is still tidying to do"

effects.log: She laughs, a landslide of a laugh, and gets up, and goes north to move a lake. Some peers just need a reason.

events.text: In a lake in the next province lives an Imugi that has waited three thousand years to become a dragon, and never has. Each time it was about to rise, someone saw it, or a storm failed, or heaven was busy. It has heard of you. It would like to know, as one old thing to another, whether it is worth going on waiting.

choices.text: "Yes. Waiting is not failing"

effects.log: The Imugi sinks back into its lake, and for the first time in a thousand years it sleeps without dreaming of the sky.

choices.text: "No. Stop waiting. Be what you are, here"

effects.log: The Imugi is silent a long time, then laughs, which makes the lake slosh over its banks. It becomes the guardian of that lake and is loved there for another three thousand years. It never rises. It does not mind.

choices.text: "I will watch for you next time. No one will see you rise but me"

effects.log: It looks at you with an expression you will never forget. "Then call me when the storm is right," it says.

events.text: The storm is right. Black clouds over the next province, lightning walking on the lake, the rain coming sideways. The old Imugi is rising out of the water, slowly, three thousand years of waiting in one motion. On the shore a child has come out to see what the noise is. If the child sees, it is over again.

choices.text: Throw your shadow over the child

effects.log: The child sees only darkness and goes back inside, grumbling about the storm. Behind the dark, an old Imugi becomes a dragon at last and goes up into the cloud, and the whole sky is lit green for a moment. You hear it thank you from a very great height.

choices.text: Let the child see. Some things must be risked, and witnessed

effects.log: The child sees, and points, and shouts. "Dragon!" And the old Imugi, hearing itself named dragon, rises anyway. A child's word was the right word after all. Nobody had ever thought of that before.

events.text: A quiet year. You find yourself counting the kingdoms you have watched rise and fall from this mountain. The count comes out differently each time, because some ended slowly and some were really two, and one was only ever a rebellion with a good flag.

choices.text: Count them by their founders

effects.log: Brave, all of them, and most of them liars, and every one certain the dynasty would last ten thousand years. You liked several of them. You remember the young faces best.

choices.text: Count them by their famines

effects.log: It is a darker list, and more honest. Kingdoms end, mostly, when the rice ends. You resolve, again, to watch the rice.

choices.text: Stop counting. Count the cranes on the river instead

effects.log: Forty-one cranes. Next year, thirty-eight. The year after, fifty. It is a much more satisfying history.

events.text: At the autumn festival in the valley a storyteller with a fan and a drummer is performing the legend of the great beast of the mountain. You. It is completely wrong. In this version you ate a general, married a princess, and were born from an egg laid by the moon. The crowd loves it.

choices.text: Let the legend be. It is theirs now

effects.log: You listen to the whole performance, through three encores. The princess part is the best. You go home and find yourself humming the drummer's refrain for a decade.

choices.text: Visit the storyteller that night and correct the facts

effects.log: The storyteller listens politely, nods, takes notes, and next year performs the princess version again, with one of your corrections added as a new scene. It is still wrong. It is better.

choices.text: Send a gentle gust that flips the storyteller's fan at the princess part

effects.log: The crowd thinks it is part of the show. It becomes part of the show. For three hundred years, storytellers flip their fans at the princess part. Nobody knows why.

events.text: The king is seven. The regents fight over the child like dogs over a bone. One night the child king climbs out of the palace through a gap in the back wall, all the way up the hill behind it, and sits on a rock under your mountain in a red robe much too big. {npc} is not crying. {npc} is very, very angry.

choices.text: "Tell me who is cruel to you. All of them"

mem.note: listened to me on the hill

effects.log: {npc} names nine people. The next morning, nine people in the palace wake to find great furrows in the earth outside their doors, which you did not quite intend. The regents behave very carefully for a decade.

choices.text: Teach {npc} to be patient

effects.log: It is a long night. You tell {npc} about the reeds and the flood, about which plants survive. {npc} goes back down before dawn and waits eleven years, and then takes the government in one morning, without bloodshed.

choices.text: Carry {npc} back to bed, and say nothing

effects.log: {npc} falls asleep on the way. In the morning the palace swears it was a dream. {npc} does not, and climbs the hill once a year for the rest of the reign, just to sit on the rock.

events.text: The new dynasty is carving the whole sky into a stone slab: every star of the twenty-eight mansions, copied from an old rubbing of a chart lost in a river a thousand years ago. The chief astronomer has noticed that one cluster of stars has moved since the old chart was made. Or something has moved in front of it.

choices.text: "The stars have moved. A thousand years is long, even for stars"

effects.log: The astronomer corrects the stars and carves the date beside them. It is the most accurate chart in the world for three hundred years.

choices.text: "I have been in the way. I will move"

effects.log: That night you lie elsewhere. The cluster reappears. The astronomer carves it and then, in the empty corner of the slab, carves something small and vague that nobody ever explains.

events.text: A young beast has come to your mountain: small, hungry, hunted, with the faint glow of something that will one day be what you are. It does not know what it is. Nobody told it. Neither did anyone tell you, once.

choices.text: Let it stay, and teach it to hide

effects.log: It stays a hundred years, a hundred years of small questions, and leaves one spring for a mountain of its own. It never writes. Young things do not. It sends a storm in your direction every few decades, which is the same thing.

choices.text: Send it away. Every great beast must climb alone

effects.log: It goes, looking back. You are not sure you were right. You are sure that you were not raised, and you are still here. That proves less than you would like it to.

choices.text: Tell it every danger you ever met, and let it choose

effects.log: It listens to your whole life in a night, terrified and delighted, and leaves at dawn with a hundred warnings and no fear at all. That is how the young do it.

events.text: A great power has risen in the west, in its own mountains, and the villages there tell stories about it. One of them is about an old beast in the east who took it in when it was small. The power sends you, by a flock of cranes, a single word: Teacher.

choices.text: Send back: "Peer"

effects.log: The cranes carry it west. That year the rains in the west and the east come at the same time, as if two powers had agreed it between them.

choices.text: Send back nothing, and be quietly proud

effects.log: You do not reply. The young one did not expect a reply. Some things are complete in one word.

events.text: A young person comes up your mountain with a family register so old the paper is brown. Twenty-six generations back, an ancestor's name has a strange note beside it: friend of the mountain. {npc} has walked four days to ask if it is true, and what that ancestor was like.

choices.text: Tell {npc} everything you remember

effects.log: You remember a laugh, a habit of humming off-key, a way of bowing too fast. {npc} laughs, because {npc} has the same laugh. Twenty-six generations, and the laugh survived.

choices.text: "It is true. The rest is yours to find"

effects.log: {npc} spends a year in the archives and comes back with a whole life, wrong in places. You correct one detail. {npc} writes the book anyway.

choices.text: "Your ancestor would want you to be your own friend of the mountain"

effects.log: {npc} comes back every year after that. In the family register, the note is copied beside a second name.

events.text: The oldest whale in the eastern sea has come to the cliffs below you to die. It is older than you are, just barely, and it wants to tell someone what the sea was like before there were kingdoms on the shore.

choices.text: Listen, for as long as it takes

effects.log: It takes a season. The sea before kingdoms was very quiet, and the fish were very large, and the whale's mother sang a song that no living thing now knows except you. When it is done, the whale goes down and does not come up.

choices.text: Ask about the other great ones it met

effects.log: It met many. Most are gone into mountains or rivers or the sky. A few are still out there. It names them, and where, and you realise how small the world of the great ones has become.

choices.text: Ask the divers to keep its bones from the traders

effects.log: The divers guard the beach for a month. The bones are buried on the headland, and the divers hold a rite there every year, and nobody remembers why except that it was asked.

events.text: The last beast hunter of a family that has hunted great beasts for forty generations has come to your mountain alone. The family's records say you are the last one worth hunting. {npc} is old, has no children, and wants to end the family's work properly. "One way or the other," {npc} says.

choices.text: Fight {npc} fairly, as the family deserves

ok.log: It is a good fight, short and real. When {npc} is down, you do not finish it. {npc} lies in the snow and laughs. "Forty generations," {npc} says. "And it ends with a beast being polite." {npc} goes home and burns the records.

fail.deathCause: the last spear of a forty-generation hunting family
fail.log: Forty generations of practice are in the spear.

choices.text: "Your family has hunted long enough. Stay a winter, and tell me about them"

effects.log: {npc} stays the winter in a cave on your mountain, telling stories of forty generations of hunts, some of which were about you. In spring {npc} leaves the spear behind, stuck in the snow, and goes south.

choices.text: Show {npc} the graves of the great beasts the family killed

effects.log: There are many. {npc} visits every one, alone, over a year. When {npc} is done, {npc} does not come back to your mountain. That is an answer.

events.text: The valley's great festival is in your honour, and it has changed. Four hundred years ago it was a solemn rite of thanks for rain. Now there are masked dancers, a straw figure of you that looks like a confused ox, wrestling, rice cakes, and a great deal of drinking. Nobody prays any more. Everyone is very happy.

choices.text: Send a light rain at the end, the old way

effects.log: A gentle rain at sunset. The old people, who remember the rite from their grandparents, kneel in it. The young people dance in it. Both are right.

choices.text: Enjoy it exactly as it is

effects.log: You watch all three days. The straw figure is very bad. You love it. At the end they burn it, and the smoke goes up past you, and you take in a little of the festival.

choices.text: Steal the straw figure on the last night

effects.log: In the morning the straw figure is on your summit, neatly arranged, looking out over the valley. The village is delighted. It becomes part of the festival, sending the figure up the mountain. You have to keep doing it now.

events.text: You have had many names. The first humans who saw you gave you one; each kingdom renamed you; the monks had one, the shamans another, the court a title. Tonight an old mudang at the foot of your mountain is calling all of them, in order, from a scroll her family has kept for nine hundred years. She stops at the last. "What should the next one be?" she asks.

choices.text: "The one the first humans gave me"

effects.log: She writes the first name again at the bottom of the scroll. It is a small plain word, a farmer's word. It suits you better than any of the titles did.

choices.text: "None. Let the next ones find me without a name"

effects.log: She leaves the space blank and rolls up the scroll. Her granddaughter will call you only "the mountain", and that, it turns out, is enough.

choices.text: Tell her the name you call yourself

effects.log: She writes it, in characters that do not quite fit it, and promises never to say it aloud. She never does. The scroll keeps it, the last name on a very long list.

events.text: You have become a pilgrimage. Pilgrims from three kingdoms climb your mountain every spring, tie ribbons to the pines, and leave prayers on paper in the cracks of the rocks. There are thousands of prayers. Most of them are about children, debts and rain. One of them, in a child's hand, asks you to come down and play.

choices.text: Answer the rain prayers

effects.log: It is the one kind you can actually answer. The spring rains come on time in three kingdoms. The pilgrims double the next year, which is a mixed blessing.

choices.text: Answer the child's prayer

effects.log: One small pilgrim, separated from the group, spends an afternoon playing hide-and-seek with a very large shadow among the rocks, and wins, because you let the child win. Nobody believes the story. The child does not care.

choices.text: Read every prayer, and answer none

effects.log: It takes a year. You learn more about humans from their prayers than from three thousand years of watching them. What they want, mostly, is to be less afraid.

events.text: Heaven has decided you are ready. A stair of light comes down onto your summit, and at the top of it there is a seat waiting among the powers. Not yet an order; an invitation. Below you, the valley you have watched for ages is lighting its evening fires.

choices.text: Climb a few steps, look back, and come down again

effects.log: From the tenth step, the valley looks like a handful of embers. From the twentieth, you cannot see the faces. You come down. Heaven, which has seen this before, leaves the stair where it is.

choices.text: "Not until the valley no longer needs me"

effects.log: The stair fades slowly, as if reluctant. That night a child in the valley dreams of a golden staircase and a voice saying "not yet", and wakes up comforted for no reason.

choices.text: Ask heaven what the seat is for

effects.log: There is a long pause from the top of the stair, as if nobody has ever asked. Then an official says, a little defensively: "Watching." You already do that. You stay where you are.
